title: Need for better evaluation methods for generative models
description: Advances in generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood directly motivate further research into how to evaluate such models.
canonical_description: generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood need better evaluation methods

evidence.anchor: motivate further research into how to evaluate such models
evidence.quote:
Advances in generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood directly motivate further research
into how to evaluate such models.

verdict.reasoning: Several papers make genuine contributions toward evaluating generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood, yet none solves the full breadth of the gap. Paper 4 (GM Score) is labeled a direct solution and explicitly targets models without likelihood estimates, but it is validated only on MNIST with GANs and requires labeled data and pre-trained classifiers — leaving open the question of domain-agnostic, unsupervised, or non-image evaluation. Paper 1 (LeGAN) leverages GAN discriminator embeddings, which is clever but architecture-specific and not transferable to diffusion models, VAEs, or autoregressive models. Paper 2 systematically studies existing GAN metrics but proposes no new method. Paper 3 proposes metrics but restricts to tabular data. Paper 5 tackles visual models with an LLM-based agent but only covers images/video. Collectively, these papers advance evaluation methodology across multiple sub-domains (GANs, tabular, visual), but the core gap — a general, principled, model-agnostic evaluation framework applicable across the full spectrum of likelihood-free generative models — remains open. No single paper or combination fully covers all model types (diffusion, autoregressive, energy-based, VAEs with intractable likelihoods) across diverse modalities (text, audio, 3D, molecular, etc.) without relying on domain-specific infrastructure.

paper.title: Likelihood Estimation for Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: We present a simple method for assessing the quality of generated images in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The method can be applied in any kind of GAN without interfering with the learning procedure or affecting the learning objective. The central idea is to define a likelihood function that correlates with the quality of the generated images. In particular, we derive a Gaussian likelihood function from the distribution of the embeddings (hidden activations) of the real images in the discriminator, and based on this, define two simple measures of how likely it is that the embeddings of generated images are from the distribution of the embeddings of the real images. This yields a simple measure of fitness for generated images, for all varieties of GANs. Empirical results on CIFAR-10 demonstrate a strong correlation between the proposed measures and the perceived quality of the generated images.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes LeGAN, a method to evaluate GANs by fitting a Gaussian distribution to the discriminator's embeddings of real images and then measuring how likely the embeddings of generated (fake) images are under that distribution. Two specific measures are introduced: ℓ_diff (likelihood difference) and ℓ_ratio (likelihood ratio). The paper demonstrates empirically on CIFAR-10 that these measures correlate with perceived image quality for vanilla GANs and LSGANs, and also correlate with the Wasserstein distance in Wasserstein GANs.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper only addresses evaluation for GANs, not for the broader class of generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood (e.g., diffusion models, energy-based models, autoregressive models with intractable likelihoods, VAEs with marginal likelihood intractability). The proposed method is inherently tied to the GAN architecture — it requires a discriminator network with access to its internal embeddings, which does not exist in other generative model families. Additionally, the method assumes the discriminator embeddings are approximately Gaussian (via central limit theorem), which may not hold universally. The paper also does not provide a standardized, model-agnostic evaluation benchmark or protocol that could be applied across different types of generative models.
evidence_snippets: We present a simple method for assessing the quality of generated images in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs). The method can be applied in any kind of GAN without interfering with the learning procedure or affecting the learning objective.

In this paper, we propose Likelihood Estimation for Generative Adversarial Networks (LeGAN), a general measure of goodness, based on a likelihood function defined for the discriminator, which can be applied to any kind of GAN.

Although GANs are able to learn the Probability Density Function (PDF) underlying a set of real images, they can not explicitly provide a likelihood for (i.e., effectively evaluate) this estimated PDF.

paper.title: An empirical study on evaluation metrics of generative adversarial networks
paper.abstract: Evaluating generative adversarial networks (GANs) is inherently challenging. In this paper, we revisit several representative sample-based evaluation metrics for GANs, and address the problem of how to evaluate the evaluation metrics. We start with a few necessary conditions for metrics to produce meaningful scores, such as distinguishing real from generated samples, identifying mode dropping and mode collapsing, and detecting overfitting. With a series of carefully designed experiments, we comprehensively investigate existing sample-based metrics and identify their strengths and limitations in practical settings. Based on these results, we observe that kernel Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and the 1-Nearest-Neighbor (1-NN) two-sample test seem to satisfy most of the desirable properties, provided that the distances between samples are computed in a suitable feature space. Our experiments also unveil interesting properties about the behavior of several popular GAN models, such as whether they are memorizing training samples, and how far they are from learning the target distribution.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper systematically evaluates existing sample-based evaluation metrics (Inception Score, Mode Score, Kernel MMD, Wasserstein distance, FID, 1-NN two-sample test) for GANs. It proposes necessary conditions for good metrics (discriminability, sensitivity to mode collapse/dropping, robustness to transformations, sample efficiency, ability to detect overfitting) and tests existing metrics against these criteria. It finds that MMD and 1-NN two-sample test perform best when distances are computed in a suitable feature space (e.g., a pre-trained ResNet). The paper provides practical recommendations for which metrics to use and releases code for the community.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not propose new evaluation methods — it evaluates existing ones. It also does not address the broader gap of how to design fundamentally better evaluation methods for generative models beyond GANs (e.g., diffusion models, autoregressive models, VAEs). The study is limited to GANs and image datasets, and the recommendations (MMD, 1-NN in a suitable feature space) are empirical observations rather than a principled theoretical framework for evaluation. The paper also does not solve the problem of evaluation when no pre-trained feature extractor is available or appropriate for the domain.
evidence_snippets: In this paper we comprehensively examine the existing literature on sample-based quantitative evaluation of GANs. We address the challenge of evaluating the metrics themselves by carefully designing a series of experiments through which we hope to answer the following questions: 1) What are reasonable characterizations of the behavior of existing sample-based metrics for GANs? 2) What are the strengths and limitations of these metrics, and which metrics should be preferred accordingly?

Our empirical observation suggests that MMD and 1-NN two-sample test are best suited as evaluation metrics on the basis of satisfying useful properties such as discriminating real versus fake images, sensitivity to mode dropping and collapse, and computational efficiency.

Overall, our empirical study suggests that the choice of feature space in which to compute various metrics is crucial. In the convolutional space of a ResNet pretrained on ImageNet, both MMD and 1-NN accuracy appear to be good metrics in terms of discriminability, robustness and efficiency.

paper.title: Evaluating Generative Models for Tabular Data: Novel Metrics and Benchmarking
paper.abstract: Generative models have revolutionized multiple domains, yet their application to tabular data remains underexplored. Evaluating generative models for tabular data presents unique challenges due to structural complexity, large-scale variability, and mixed data types, making it difficult to intuitively capture intricate patterns. Existing evaluation metrics offer only partial insights, lacking a comprehensive measure of generative performance. To address this limitation, we propose three novel evaluation metrics: FAED, FPCAD, and RFIS. Our extensive experimental analysis, conducted on three standard network intrusion detection datasets, compares these metrics with established evaluation methods such as Fidelity, Utility, TSTR, and TRTS. Our results demonstrate that FAED effectively captures generative modeling issues overlooked by existing metrics. While FPCAD exhibits promising performance, further refinements are necessary to enhance its reliability. Our proposed framework provides a robust and practical approach for assessing generative models in tabular data applications.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes three novel evaluation metrics (FAED, FPCAD, RFIS) specifically designed for generative models applied to tabular data. These metrics operate on samples from generative models (comparing real vs. generated distributions via Fréchet distance on latent representations, or analyzing generated samples alone via entropy-based scoring), which is exactly the paradigm needed for models that can sample but not estimate likelihood. The paper validates these metrics by injecting controlled distortions (noise, mode drop, mode collapse) into real datasets and testing whether the metrics detect them, showing FAED is the most robust.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper addresses the evaluation gap only for the specific domain of tabular data (and only tested on network intrusion detection datasets). The broader gap — needing better evaluation methods for generative models in general (images, text, audio, video, time series, etc.) — remains open. The proposed metrics are tailored to tabular data characteristics (mixed numerical/categorical types, PCA/Autoencoder latent spaces) and are not shown to generalize to other data modalities. Additionally, the paper does not provide a theoretical framework for what properties an ideal evaluation metric for sample-only generative models should have; it offers empirical comparisons on a narrow set of datasets.
evidence_snippets: Evaluating generative models for tabular data presents unique challenges due to structural complexity, large-scale variability, and mixed data types, making it difficult to intuitively capture intricate patterns.
Inspired by IS and FID, we introduce three novel evaluation metrics, FAED, FPCAD, and RFIS, tailored for assessing generative models in tabular data.

Our extensive experimental analysis, conducted on three standard network intrusion detection datasets, compares these metrics with established evaluation methods such as Fidelity, Utility, TSTR, and TRTS.

paper.title: GM Score: Incorporating inter-class and intra-class generator diversity, discriminability of disentangled representation, and sample fidelity for evaluating GANs
paper.abstract: While generative adversarial networks (GAN) are popular for their higher sample quality as opposed to other generative models like the variational autoencoders (VAE) and Boltzmann machines, they suffer from the same difficulty of the evaluation of generated samples. Various aspects must be kept in mind, such as the quality of generated samples, the diversity of classes (within a class and among classes), the use of disentangled latent spaces, agreement of said evaluation metric with human perception, etc. In this paper, we propose a new score, namely, GM Score, which takes into various factors such as sample quality, disentangled representation, intra-class and inter-class diversity, and other metrics such as precision, recall, and F1 score are employed for discriminability of latent space of deep belief network (DBN) and restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM). The evaluation is done for different GANs (GAN, DCGAN, BiGAN, CGAN, CoupledGAN, LSGAN, SGAN, WGAN, and WGAN Improved) trained on the benchmark MNIST dataset.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper directly addresses the gap by proposing a novel evaluation metric (GM Score) specifically designed for generative models that cannot estimate likelihood directly, such as GANs. The metric combines inter-class diversity, intra-class diversity (to detect mode collapse), sample fidelity via DBN/RBM feature extraction and classifier ensembles, and latent space discriminability. The paper explicitly motivates the need for such metrics by noting that GANs lack an explicit likelihood measure (Section 2), and it compares the proposed metric against existing alternatives like Inception Score and FID, showing how GM Score overcomes their shortcomings.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully addresses the gap as stated — it proposes a better evaluation method for generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood. However, the evaluation is limited to the MNIST dataset and a specific set of GAN architectures. The paper acknowledges this limitation and claims domain independence but does not empirically validate on other datasets (e.g., CIFAR-10, CelebA) or other types of generative models (e.g., VAEs, autoregressive models). Additionally, the metric relies on labeled data and pre-trained classifiers, which may limit applicability to unsupervised or non-image domains.
evidence_snippets: In this paper, we propose a new evaluation metric for GANs, namely, the *GM Score*.

Historically, the evaluation of deep generative models has been a difficult task due to several reasons. While implicit density estimation-based generative models like the deep Boltzmann machines and variational autoencoders (VAE) tend to maximize log-likelihood, giving us a measure of model performance, GANs tackle the maximization of likelihood in terms of training the objective for the discriminator. Hence, without an explicit likelihood measure, one has to look at other parameters for evaluating GANs.
We propose a novel metric for GAN evaluation (also applicable to generative models in general that are used for data generation).

paper.title: Evaluation Agent: Efficient and Promptable Evaluation Framework for Visual Generative Models
paper.abstract: Recent advancements in visual generative models have enabled high-quality image and video generation, opening diverse applications. However, evaluating these models often demands sampling hundreds or thousands of images or videos, making the process computationally expensive, especially for diffusion-based models with inherently slow sampling. Moreover, existing evaluation methods rely on rigid pipelines that overlook specific user needs and provide numerical results without clear explanations. In contrast, humans can quickly form impressions of a model's capabilities by observing only a few samples. To mimic this, we propose the Evaluation Agent framework, which employs human-like strategies for efficient, dynamic, multi-round evaluations using only a few samples per round, while offering detailed, user-tailored analyses. It offers four key advantages: 1) efficiency, 2) promptable evaluation tailored to diverse user needs, 3) explainability beyond single numerical scores, and 4) scalability across various models and tools. Experiments show that Evaluation Agent reduces evaluation time to 10% of traditional methods while delivering comparable results. The Evaluation Agent framework is fully open-sourced to advance research in visual generative models and their efficient evaluation.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes the Evaluation Agent framework, an LLM-powered agent system that evaluates visual generative models (text-to-image and text-to-video) using a human-like, dynamic, multi-round strategy with few samples. It addresses the need for efficient evaluation of generative models that sample but cannot estimate likelihood (like diffusion models) by reducing evaluation time to ~10% of traditional benchmarks while maintaining comparable accuracy. It also provides explainable, natural-language evaluation results tailored to user queries, overcoming the rigidity of fixed benchmarks.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper only addresses evaluation of visual generative models (images and videos), leaving out other types of generative models that can sample but not estimate likelihood (e.g., text generation models, audio generation, 3D generation, molecular generation, etc.). The method also relies heavily on LLM/VLM capabilities and existing evaluation toolkits, which have their own limitations and biases. The evaluation is approximate (categorizing into 5 tiers) rather than providing precise numerical scores, and the approach's effectiveness depends on the quality of the underlying LLM and evaluation tools. The gap of developing general-purpose evaluation methods that work across diverse generative model types remains open.
evidence_snippets: Recent advancements in visual generative models have enabled high-quality image and video generation, opening diverse applications. However, evaluating these models often demands sampling hundreds or thousands of images or videos, making the process computationally expensive, especially for diffusion-based models with inherently slow sampling.
We propose the Evaluation Agent, a human-like evaluation framework that overcomes the limitations of existing methods in flexibility and efficiency.

Our primary contribution is introducing a new evaluation paradigm. We are confident that the utility of the Evaluation Agent framework will continue to improve as stronger LLMs and more human-aligned evaluation toolkits are developed.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: The gap is moderately tractable but has significant challenges. On the positive side: (1) abundant data exists across modalities for testing evaluation methods; (2) compute requirements are modest — developing metrics typically requires only pre-trained feature extractors or simple statistics, not frontier-scale training; (3) there are clear baselines (FID, IS, Precision/Recall) to extend and compare against; (4) progress is measurable via correlation with human judgment, downstream task performance, or known failure-mode detection. However, the full ambition — a model-agnostic, domain-agnostic, unsupervised evaluation framework covering all likelihood-free models (diffusion, autoregressive, energy-based, VAEs) across all modalities (text, audio, 3D, molecules) — is extremely broad and would require solving fundamental issues like what constitutes a universal representation quality space. Partial/sub-problem progress (e.g., extending beyond GAN-centric metrics to cover diffusion models, or unifying evaluation across 2-3 modalities) is quite tractable with existing methods like kernel MMD, classifier two-sample tests, or learned embeddings. A small team can make meaningful headway by scoping to a well-defined subset of the gap, but fully resolving the gap as stated would require sustained, multi-group effort.
